title: Adaptive fractional slab coalescer and GPU-windowed KV reclaimer
creator: Ava Martinez
description:
Problem: As sustained continuous-batching traffic increases, the KV cache on GPUs fragments into many small unallocatable holes and underutilized micro-slabs. This results in elevated OOMs during peak sequences, suboptimal packing for long-context workloads, and unpredictable latency spikes when background compaction competes with inference kernels.

Goals:
- Reduce fragmentation and improve long-term utilization of per-GPU KV memory without introducing large stop-the-world compactions.
- Make allocation decisions GPU-aware (respecting current kernel occupancy and memory-access patterns) and batching-aware (avoiding contention during hot batching windows).
- Provide observable heuristics and safe rollouts that let us measure end-to-end latency, tail latency, and per-token cost changes.

Proposed approach (high level):
- Fractional Slab Pools: Keep the current slab allocator but introduce fractional slabs: instead of fixed-size slabs always split by model/key-size power-of-two, allow 1/2 and 1/4 slab views that can be coalesced on demand. Fractional slabs let us serve many small KV entries while preserving the ability to coalesce into larger contiguous ranges for long-context cache pinning.
- Epoch-based Lightweight Coalescer: Run a low-priority background coalescer that operates in short epochs (100–250ms quanta). During each epoch the coalescer reorders free fractional slabs into larger free runs using only adjacent free-fragment metadata and avoids moving live KV entries. These operations are strictly metadata-only (no copy) and expose extended free ranges to the allocator.
- GPU-windowed Reclaimer: When kernel occupancy is low (identified by a short, policy-driven window after batches drain), we schedule short reclamation passes that perform pointer indirection toggles to migrate cold KV entries off hot GPU pools or to promote contiguous free runs. The window avoids contention with heavy-serving periods and uses internal backpressure signals to abort if scheduling latency increases.
- Hot/Cold Tagging with Access Sampling: Each KV entry receives a lightweight decaying hotness score sampled from access hooks used by continuous batching. Entries flagged as cold become candidates for relocation or compression. Hot entries are protected from relocation for a configurable grace period.
- Adaptive Allocation Policy: The allocator uses a small on-device ML-inspired predictor (logistic heuristic) that estimates the probability an allocation will be short-lived. Allocations predicted to be ephemeral are routed to a compacting tier that uses denser packing heuristics; long-lived allocations are placed in slabs that favor coalescing. The predictor trains from lightweight counters (age, access frequency, allocation size).

Design details and invariants: 
- Metadata layout remains contiguous and memory-compact (metadata per slab is 16–24 bytes). All coalescer and reclaimer decisions are reversible and can be preempted.
- No cross-GPU blocking: Coalescing is local to a GPU's KV pool; cross-GPU migration only occurs when a node-level policy elects to rebalance (future work).
- Safety: Background passes never evict live entries; they only reorganize free ranges and mark cold entries for optional relocation. Any relocation flow uses two-phase updates with atomic pointers and epoch barriers so inference read paths remain lockless.
- Interaction with continuous batching: Allocation windows are throttled when batch queues exceed a threshold. The reclaimer watches the batching scheduler hook and yields if average batch latency rises above a guardrail.

Telemetry and observability:
- New metrics: fractional_slab_utilization, fractional_coalescer_runs, average_free_run_length, reclaimed_bytes_per_epoch, relocation_rate, eviction_pressure, hotness_distribution.
- Alerts: reclaimed_bytes_per_epoch >> baseline OR increase in OOMs after push triggers an alert.
- Benchmarks to collect: 99/99.9 tail latency for generation workloads, per-token cost, KV hit-rate, memory fragmentation ratio (free_runs_weighted_by_size / total_free_bytes).

Rollout plan:
1) Unit tests + microbench harness on small model (gpt-mini) to validate allocator invariants.
2) Canary on dedicated staging GPU fleet with synthetic long-context traces (10k sequences, varying lengths).
3) Gradual rollout to low-traffic host pool (10% of serving slabs) while monitoring tail-latency and OOMs for 48 hours.
4) Full rollout after two successful canaries with rollback playbook ready.

Trade-offs considered:
- Pro: Fractional slabs reduce internal fragmentation for small entries while preserving coalescing ability. Background coalescing avoids costly synchronous compactions.
- Con: Adds allocator complexity and modest metadata overhead. The adaptive predictor may mis-classify and cause extra relocations; we cap relocation rate as a safety valve.

Open questions and follow-ups:
- Should cross-GPU compaction be implemented for very long-lived pinned KV tables? (deferred)
- Evaluate whether compression (quantization of KV values) combined with fractional slabs is net-positive for typical customer token distributions.
- Tune epoch length and reclaimer windows empirically per GPU family (A100 vs H100).
acceptance_criteria: Unit tests covering fractional slab allocation/coalescing invariants pass in CI
Background coalescer runs without causing >5% increase in 99th-percentile latency under synthetic load
Reduction in fragmentation metric (median free_run_length or equivalent) by >=30% on staging for long-context traces
No increase in production OOM rate during 10% canary for 48h; per-token cost and 99th tail latency stable or improved
Telemetry dashboards created and documented; alert thresholds defined
updates: 2026-03-06: Spike completed — allocator prototype implemented in local allocator harness. Observed 28% reduction in fragmentation on toy traces. (doc: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ExampleSpike)
2026-03-09: Design review with Runtime team. Feedback: make coalescer epoch preemptible and add explicit guardrails tied to batching scheduler hooks.
2026-03-11: Initial PR opened for allocator changes: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4621 — contains fractional-slab metadata and basic coalescer loop.

2026-03-12: Benchmark results attached to PR show 12% median latency improvement for mixed-size KV workloads on A100 emulation. Still seeing small regression in worst-case relocation tail, investigating backoff tuning.

2026-03-14: Canary plan drafted and scheduled for 2026-03-20 on dedicated staging cluster. Monitoring playbook and rollback steps written in runbook: https://drive.redwood.ai/runbooks/kv-coalesce-canary
